transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
Ukrainian and Russian negotiators say they see some progress in two days of talks in
Abu Dhabi.
The discussions are mediated by the U.S.
President Trump's envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Whitcoff, say they'll travel to Moscow
now and speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Later, they'll meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Hundreds of schools in Italy, Scotland, Ireland and Northern Ireland have received bomb threats.
Children have been rushed out of their classrooms.
NPR's Sherlock reports on what appears to be the latest coordinated effort to sow chaos
and disruption in Europe.
Police in Northern Ireland said the more than 300 affected schools received the same chilling
email.
A copy of the message sent to Italian schools, seen by NPR, said, "I have prepared for this
for a long time to kill every one of you."
It said an explosive with a remote detonator had been placed in the building.
The message caused panic in schools with many evacuating.
Police in Scotland and Northern Ireland described the message as a hoax.
Italy's defense minister Guido Rosito said it was part of an effort to create panic and
disruption in European countries.
For NPR News, I'm Ruth Sherlock in London.
Prosecutors in the US have indicted three men allegedly involved in nearly 20 terror attacks
and attempted attacks in Europe and the United States.
Reporter Willem Marx has more from London about one of the alleged attacks.
The details are pretty extraordinary.
Prosecutors say that back in April, the men sat in a room and directed one of these attacks
remotely in real time over FaceTime, as you mentioned, telling the attacker when to light
and throw what seems to have been some kind of incendiary device.
And then the next day, one of the men, Mohammed Ali al-Hasami, allegedly told another man
attacking a London synagogue to, quote, "light it up like a Christmas tree."
Willem Marx reporting.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer says he's confident he'll keep his job as the top
Democrat this January when Democrats retake control of Congress.
Both independent Senator Bernie Sanders and Democrat Alyssa Slotkin have come out against
Schumer's candidacy, and Piers Alaina Moore reports.
Sanders, an independent who caucuses with the Democrats, told reporters that he believes
a major takeaway from the midterms is that voters want the party to move in a new direction.
I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck nobody who
works harder than Chuck Schumer.
But in my view, the time is now for change.
Senator Alyssa Slotkin echoed that, calling for colleagues to publicly challenge Schumer
and propose a plan for the first 100 days that makes good on voter calls to govern differently.
It comes as a handful of incoming Senate Democrats have also declined to back Schumer for the
top job.
Alaina Moore, NPR News.
It's NPR.
Today's Veterans Day, President Trump and First Lady Melania Trump will visit Arlington
National Cemetery this morning.
They'll participate in a wreath-laying ceremony.
The president will also deliver Veterans Day remarks.
The president's visit to the cemetery comes as several members of the Kennedy family have
filed a motion to join two lawsuits.
They're asking a judge to block Trump's plan to build a nearby triumphal arch.
The lawsuits say Trump's proposed arch will cover, in shadow, the Arlington gravesites
and memorials for former President John F. Kennedy and his brothers, their former U.S.
Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy, and former U.S. Senator Ted Kennedy.
The political power shift in the next Congress could have big implications for air travel.
NPR's Joel Rose reports the travel industry is bracing for the possibility of another
government shutdown.
U.S. air travelers suffered through three partial government shutdowns over the past
two years, with Republicans in charge of the White House and Congress.
Jeff Freeman, the head of the U.S. Travel Association, says it is hard to predict what
will happen.
And Democrats take control of the House and Senate next year.
The unpredictability certainly has us in the mindset of buckle up.
In past shutdowns, TSA officers and air traffic controllers sometimes did not get paid.
Many eventually called out sick and took on second jobs to pay their bills, leading to
hours-long security lines, as well as delayed and canceled flights.
Freeman says a divided government makes another shutdown more likely.
Joel Rose, NPR News, Washington.
listening to NPR.

topics.text: Ukrainian and Russian negotiators report progress in two days of talks in Abu Dhabi
Trump envoys Kushner and Witkoff head to Moscow to meet Putin, then Zelensky
Hundreds of schools in Italy, Scotland, Ireland and Northern Ireland receive bomb threat emails
Prosecutors indict three men allegedly directing nearly 20 terror attacks in Europe and US
Schumer says he expects to keep Senate Democratic leadership despite Sanders and Slotkin opposition
Trump and Melania Trump to visit Arlington Cemetery for Veterans Day wreath-laying
Kennedy family moves to join lawsuits seeking to block Trump's planned triumphal arch near Arlington
Travel industry braces for possible government shutdown under divided Congress affecting air travel
